name: Vibravox
description: A dataset of French speech captured with body-conduction audio sensors. It contains audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors and an airborne microphone used as a reference. The corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer. Annotations about the recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are included.
creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu
citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poirée, and É. Bavu, "vibravox (revision 071945b)," 2024. https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was developed through a rigorous data collection process. The authors designed and implemented a recording protocol, assembled the necessary hardware, and built dedicated software to ensure a controlled and high-quality data acquisition setup. Recordings were made with six sensors simultaneously: five body-conduction microphones and one airborne headset microphone as reference. For each participant, four steps were performed consecutively: speech-clean (15 minutes of reading sentences sourced from French Wikipedia), speechless-noisy (2 minutes 24 seconds remaining silent in 3D spatialized ambient noise), speechless-clean (54 seconds in silence to record physiological and sensor noise), and speech-noisy (54 seconds of reading in noisy conditions using in-house ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events). Ambient noise was rendered around participants using a spherical array of 56 loudspeakers.
rai:dataCollectionType: Direct measurement, Experiments, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Document analysis
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: A small number of audio clips had shortcomings such as mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from their initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, or a microphone inadvertently left unequipped, leading to data inconsistencies. Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained after post-processing, and 28,471 sentences were kept from an initial 30,568. The post-processing excluded 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of simultaneous 6-channel audio recordings captured by a Zoom F8n field recorder at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution from a headset microphone, forehead accelerometer, in-ear soft foam microphone, in-ear rigid earpiece microphone, throat microphone, and temple vibration pickup. Text read by participants came from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Ambient noise samples were sourced largely from AudioSet and from in-house ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The text utilized for participant readings was filtered to produce a simplified dataset with a minimum number of textual and phonemic symbols and to minimize pronunciation uncertainty. Utterances containing most proper names, numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, or syntactic errors were removed. Text was normalized by lowercasing and removing punctuation except apostrophes. Phonetic transcriptions were generated and manually corrected for some unrecognized words. The dataset was split by speaker, with 80% of male and female speakers in training, 10% in validation, and 10% in test, ensuring no speaker overlap between splits.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter was uniformly applied to each acquisition channel during recording. Post-processing applied three automatic filters to speech-clean utterances: keeping only samples with phoneme error rate below 10%, signal-to-noise ratio greater than 1.5 dB, and speech level above the mean silence level for the sensor. Indicators were extracted using whisper-timestamped for word timestamps and voice activity detection, Levenshtein distance for phoneme error rate, and percentile sound levels for speech and silence. If a speech-clean sample passed all filters, voice activity detection timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides; if adjusted boundaries exceeded the original audio, the audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side to remove artifacts such as mouse clicks. All recordings from the other three subsets were kept if the corresponding participant had a non-empty speech-clean subset.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations include recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions. Sentences read by participants were sourced from filtered and normalized French Wikipedia text from Common Voice. From this normalized text, corresponding phonetic transcriptions using the International Phonetic Alphabet were generated with the text phonemizer of the CoML lab. For some words where the phonemizer produced language switches, manual phonetic transcription was performed. During speech-clean recording, each utterance generated a new recording and the transcriptions were retained.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To ensure high-quality labels for the speech-to-phonemes task, the authors computed phoneme error rate for each sample using the Levenshtein distance between the phonetic labeled transcription and the phonetic transcription derived from Whisper output. Samples with phoneme error rate above 10% were discarded. This was used to address potential discrepancies between the labeled transcription and actual pronunciation.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: CoML lab text phonemizer; whisper-timestamped model based on Whisper
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes participant gender and age statistics. The paper also notes that the speechless-clean subset can be valuable for tasks such as heart rate tracking and that the rich biometric data may include heart rate and breathing. Speaker identity is also inherent in the voice recordings.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors hope the release will drive progress in body-conducted speech analysis and support the development of robust communication systems for real-world applications. The paper discusses applications in noisy environments, military operations, industrial settings, access control, intelligence gathering, voice commands, monitoring vital signs including heart rate, and battlefield forensics involving emotional states and life signals.
rai:dataBiases: To increase representativeness and inclusivity, a deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants. The dataset was split by speaker with 80% of male and female speakers in training, 10% in validation, and 10% in test. The paper also notes that some sensors, especially in-ear microphones, may suffer from inadequate acoustic sealing for certain ear canal anatomies, and that individual variance influences transmission of external noise through the device.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is in French, which limits language coverage. Although not the largest BCM dataset, it contains 45 hours per sensor. The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes because it lacks a clean reference under noisy conditions. Post-processing excluded 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences to ensure rigorous analysis rather than maximize overall performance. Some cases such as a participant's ear canal being too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing were not always detected by the filters. The paper also notes that body-conduction sensors have reduced bandwidth and that different sensors present trade-offs between noise robustness and frequency range.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, validation, and testing of speech-related tasks including speech enhancement, bandwidth extension, speech-to-phonemes recognition, and speaker verification. The speech-clean subset contains the most data for training. The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes. The speechless-noisy subset can be combined with speech-clean recordings for data augmentation to simulate noisy scenarios while retaining a clean reference. The speechless-clean subset can be used for tasks such as heart rate tracking, analyzing sensor noise properties, or generating synthetic datasets with realistic physiological and sensor-inherent noise.
